bp: A conversational recommender is trying to help a person choose something through back-and-forth talk rather than through a one-shot search box. The useful object is not just the final item list; it is the system's live guess about what the person wants right now. Past conversations can be valuable because they show old preferences, repeated constraints, and ways the user explained likes or dislikes. EyeCRS starts from the uncomfortable fact that more personal history is not always better. A user's old dialogue about one need can push the recommender away from the current need, like using last month's restaurant discussion to guide today's laptop choice. The paper serves systems that personalize in real time but must decide which memories deserve influence. Its central question is therefore practical: before adding historical dialogue to a current recommendation, can the system judge whether that history will help or hurt the decision?
wh: The hard part is that history has two faces. It can clarify stable preference, but it can also carry stale goals, unrelated situations, and old wording that looks personal while being irrelevant. Existing methods described in the abstract often use the whole historical dialogue record without discrimination. That is tempting because a larger user record seems richer. The failure is cognitive negative transfer: a past session transfers the wrong mental frame into the current decision, so the system becomes personalized in the wrong direction. In conversation, this is especially damaging because the system must respond immediately while the user is still revealing intent. The current dialogue may be short, ambiguous, or incomplete, so old sessions can dominate simply because they contain more text. The central tension is personalization versus contamination. The system needs memory, but it needs a way to inspect memory before letting it reshape the recommendation.
naive: A smart beginner would collect every prior dialogue from the user, attach it to the current conversation, and let the recommender infer a richer preference profile. If the user once discussed price, brand, genre, or comfort, the system could reuse those clues. This fails when the old dialogue belongs to a different decision context. A helpful clue in one session can become a misleading cue in another. The beginner's system has no courtroom where history must justify itself; it treats all remembered sessions as friendly evidence. EyeCRS is built around the opposite assumption: every piece of personal history should be tested because some remembered information actively reduces recommendation quality.
ap: The core idea is to put a gate in front of personalization. EyeCRS does not simply pour the user's historical dialogues into the downstream recommender. It first stages a debate over each historical session's role in the current decision. One side argues that a past dialogue supports the present recommendation, while the opposing side argues that it may introduce cognitive negative transfer. This debate is inspired by behavioral decision theory, which treats decision quality as something shaped by competing reasons, biases, and context rather than by raw information volume. Only the historical dialogues judged positive move forward. Then the Parametric Injection Module turns those validated dialogues into model-side knowledge and injects them into the downstream recommender's internal settings. In plain terms, the paper filters memory before teaching the recommender from it.
mech: The mechanism begins with two inputs: the user's current conversational recommendation state and the user's historical dialogue records. First, EyeCRS treats each old dialogue session as a candidate source of personal knowledge, not as automatically trusted context. Second, the Multi-Agent Debate Module creates opposing evaluations. A supporting agent searches for reasons that the old session reflects useful preference for the current choice. An opposing agent searches for reasons that the same session could pull the recommender toward the wrong decision. Third, the debate produces a judgment about whether that historical session is positive or harmful for the current recommendation. The abstract does not specify the exact scoring formula, so the safe interpretation is that the debate functions as a rigorous relevance-and-risk filter. Fourth, EyeCRS keeps the sessions validated as positive and discards or downplays sessions likely to cause negative transfer. Fifth, the Parametric Injection Module parameterizes those accepted historical dialogues, meaning it converts their information into adjustable model-side form rather than leaving them as raw conversation text. Finally, that selected personal knowledge is injected into the downstream recommender's intrinsic parameter space, so the recommender can internalize the useful history when producing real-time recommendations.
math: The main mathematical idea is selective weighting under uncertainty. The system has many possible pieces of evidence, the historical sessions, and must decide which should affect the current recommendation. A simple average over all history assumes every session is useful. EyeCRS instead asks for a signed judgment: does this session push in a helpful direction or a harmful one? That is a relevance problem, because the old dialogue must be compared with the current decision. It is also a ranking and filtering problem, because accepted sessions receive influence while rejected sessions do not. The debate mechanism can be understood as adversarial comparison in everyday terms: one evaluator builds the case for inclusion, another builds the case for exclusion, and the system uses the clash to reduce one-sided confidence. The Parametric Injection Module uses learning from examples: accepted dialogues are transformed into settings inside the recommender, so future scoring reflects the selected preference signal. The tradeoff is personalization versus noise. Too little history makes the recommender generic; too much untested history imports stale or mismatched intent. The math fits because the useful structure is sparse: only some remembered conversations matter for the current moment.
dots: EyeCRS sits inside recommender systems, where many papers ask how to choose a small useful set from a much larger and noisier pile. Its specific pile is not products but memories. That connects it to ranking, because the recommender ultimately must order candidate items for the user. It also connects to the conference concept of focusing on what is relevant: the current decision should place weight on helpful past sessions and quiet the rest. Neighboring conversational recommendation work such as AID, described in the repo as using hypothesis-grounded probing, handles ambiguity by asking targeted questions when multiple interpretations remain plausible. MOCHA, another conversational recommendation neighbor in the current JSON data, selects item and feature knowledge before explaining a recommendation. EyeCRS solves a related deeper problem from the memory side: before recommending, decide which personal evidence should be allowed to guide the system at all.
ww: It works, if it works, because it changes the role of history from stored bulk to contested evidence. The naive system gives old dialogue power merely because it belongs to the same user. EyeCRS asks whether the old dialogue belongs to the same current decision. The supporting and opposing agents are useful because harmful history is often plausible on the surface: it contains the user's own words, so a recommender may overtrust it. A structured argument against inclusion gives the system a chance to notice mismatched context before that mismatch changes the item scores. The injection step then helps because the accepted history is not just pasted beside the current dialogue. It is turned into internal model influence, which the abstract says helps the recommender internalize personalized knowledge. The intuitive gain is sharper memory: keep the preference evidence that truly narrows the current choice, and prevent unrelated personal traces from crowding out what the user is saying now.
po: The payoff is a conversational recommender that can personalize without assuming every old conversation is beneficial. According to the full current WWW JSON in the repo, experiments on two real-world datasets show that EyeCRS mitigates cognitive negative transfer and achieves stronger conversational recommendation performance. In practical terms, the system should be better at using stable user preference while avoiding old sessions that distort the current choice. The benefit is not simply more memory. It is controlled memory: historical dialogue becomes useful only after it has passed a relevance-and-harm check.
limits: Several assumptions must hold. The debate agents must be good enough judges of when an old dialogue helps or hurts; if both sides miss a subtle context mismatch, bad history can still enter. The current dialogue must contain enough signal to compare against history. The parameter injection step assumes selected dialogues can be converted into internal recommender knowledge without overwriting useful general behavior. The abstract does not prove which kinds of past sessions are hardest to judge, how often the debate itself is wrong, or whether the gains hold for domains beyond the reported real-world datasets. It also does not detail the exact scoring rule behind the debate.
